passage:
In the canteen Swati threw her head back laughing at something Rashmi said, and Uma felt a hot pang shoot through her chest. The urge came fast: ask who Rashmi really was, ask why she had never laughed like that with her. Uma pressed her nails into her palm and did not say any of it. That night she said, "When you laughed with Rashmi today I felt a sting, and I think it's my insecurity. It isn't about what you did. I don't want to make you feel watched."

Swati had felt the watching for weeks. There had been questions after every outing, and a slightly hurt silence when she said she'd been with friends. She had even stopped mentioning Rashmi, leaving her out of stories to keep the evening calm, and she disliked how that felt. She took Uma's hand. "Thank you for telling me plainly. I love you, and there's nothing going on. I'll say that once. But I'm not going to stop seeing my friends, and I don't want to hide them either."

Uma nodded. It stung, and it was also a relief. On Saturday, Swati invited Rashmi along to the film, and Uma bought the popcorn.

qa.q: What did Swati and Rashmi do in the canteen that made Uma feel a pang?
qa.a: They laughed together, and Swati threw her head back laughing at something Rashmi said.

qa.q: How did Uma's confession and Swati's answer fit together?
qa.a: Uma named her insecurity as her own feeling instead of interrogating Swati. Swati, who had felt watched and had started hiding Rashmi, reassured her once and held the line that she would keep seeing her friends.

qa.q: What was Swati feeling in the weeks before Uma spoke plainly?
qa.a: She felt watched and uneasy, enough that she left Rashmi out of her stories to keep things calm.

qa.q: What could Uma do the next time she feels that pang?
qa.a: She can share it as her feeling rather than an accusation, and avoid questioning Swati or asking her to give up friends.

grounding: Jealousy in a relationship is seen from the partner who feels the pang and owns it and the partner who has felt watched.

passage:
When Harish got the offer from the design studio, the whole group chat lit up. Farhan typed "Congrats!" and put on a smile at the tea stall, but a small, cold feeling sat under his ribs, and he heard his own voice say, "Must be nice." Harish glanced at him, then looked away.

Harish had noticed the coolness in the last few days. The joking had slowed, and there were sarcastic little comments. He felt a pinch of hurt. He did not pretend the offer was nothing, and he did not start talking about it every five minutes either. He kept his voice normal and asked, "How's your portfolio going?" and let Farhan give a one-word answer.

That night Farhan opened his notebook and wrote, "I'm jealous." He read the line, and it looked less frightening on paper. The next line came more easily: "I want to work on products people use, not just get the same job as everybody." He closed the notebook, and the smallness eased a little.

The next morning he found Harish at the gate. "I was a jerk yesterday. I'm really glad for you, honestly. Tell me about the studio." Jomon, who had been listening, raised an eyebrow, then grinned. Harish laughed. "It has a very bad coffee machine."

qa.q: What kind of studio made Harish the offer?
qa.a: It was a design studio.

qa.q: How did Farhan's envy and Harish's response fit together, and what did the notebook change?
qa.a: Farhan smiled but said must be nice, and Harish noticed the coolness, stayed warm and did not hide his news. In the notebook Farhan admitted his envy and worked out what he wanted, so he could congratulate Harish honestly.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling at the tea stall when he typed Congrats?
qa.a: He felt small and envious while smiling, with a cold feeling under his ribs.

qa.q: What could Harish do if Farhan is still a bit distant next month?
qa.a: He can stay warm without hiding his progress, and give Farhan room and time.

grounding: A friend's job offer is seen from the friend who feels small while smiling and the friend whose success creates distance.

passage:
When the directors doubted Vinita's plan for the regional launch, Francis put his hand up in the meeting. "I'll stand behind her numbers." Vinita felt her throat tighten. She promised herself she would honour it, and over the next weeks she stayed late on the forecasts and double-checked every figure. Shalini had a similar story: Francis had hired her when two other managers turned her down for lacking a degree, and she often thought about the day he called with the offer.

Then, before a client call, Francis said, "We can promise the client delivery by the fifteenth." Vinita knew the warehouse could not do it, and her stomach dropped. Owing him so much made it awkward, but she pulled him aside. "I'm grateful for everything, and that's why I'm telling you. The fifteenth isn't realistic. Here's what the warehouse says." Shalini had the same figure and slid it onto the table. "I checked it twice."

Francis looked at the sheet for a long moment. "You're right. I should have asked first." He rang the client and gave a different date. Afterwards he said quietly, "Thank you. I'd rather hear it from you than find out on the fifteenth." Vinita and Shalini glanced at each other, and both let out a breath.

qa.q: What day did Francis want to promise the client delivery?
qa.a: He wanted to promise delivery by the fifteenth.

qa.q: How did Vinita's and Shalini's gratitude toward Francis show up in what they did when he made the promise?
qa.a: Both felt they owed him for backing them, and both still spoke up honestly about the unrealistic date, Vinita privately and Shalini with the figures. Francis valued the candid input and changed the date.

qa.q: What was Vinita feeling when Francis stood up for her plan in the meeting?
qa.a: She felt deeply grateful, with her throat tightening, and resolved to honour it.

qa.q: What could Shalini do if she sees another mistake in Francis's plans?
qa.a: She could speak up with facts and kindness, as she did with the figures, because thanks does not mean silence.

grounding: A manager's support is seen by two employees whose gratitude does not stop them from telling him he is mistaken.

passage:
Arohi found the messages on a Tuesday, in the middle of folding laundry. Her hands went numb. She sat on the bathroom floor, feeling sick, as if she no longer knew who she was married to. She did not post a word online or call Shalini's office. Instead, she rang her friend Dilnaz, who came over that night and stayed on the sofa, making tea and letting her cry. Arohi told herself, in Dilnaz's kitchen, that this was not her failing, and that she did not have to decide anything yet.

Shalini had come home and told the truth before Arohi could ask. "I have been seeing someone else. I'm ending it. I've hurt you badly." She did not say it meant nothing, and she did not say it was because of anything Arohi had done. When Arohi's voice broke in anger, Shalini stayed in the room. "You can be as angry as you need to be. Ask me anything and I'll answer." She answered every question, even the uncomfortable ones, without defending herself.

Weeks later Shalini did not ask to be forgiven. She said, "Whatever pace you need is right." Arohi looked at her a long moment and said, "I don't know yet." Shalini nodded and put the kettle on.

qa.q: Who came over that night to stay with Arohi?
qa.a: Dilnaz came over and stayed on the sofa.

qa.q: How did Shalini's honesty and Arohi's reaction fit together?
qa.a: Shalini told the truth without excuses, stayed through Arohi's anger and did not ask to be forgiven quickly. Arohi took time, leaned on Dilnaz and did not seek public revenge, leaving decisions about the future for later.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling when she sat on the bathroom floor?
qa.a: She felt shock and sickness, as if she no longer knew who she was married to.

qa.q: What could Shalini do in the following months if Arohi still has questions?
qa.a: She can keep answering honestly without defensiveness and let trust come back at Arohi's pace, not her own.

grounding: A betrayal in marriage is seen from the partner who broke trust and stays honest and the partner who takes time and leans on a friend.

passage:
Gargi knew the exact time Nazia's picture had last changed. She checked the profile before lectures, in the queue, at midnight, reading meanings into a new song on her story. The thoughts looped like a stuck record. One evening she caught herself standing at the library exit, ready to wait for Nazia to appear, and she turned around, cheeks burning. She told her friend Nandini, and Nandini said, "It sounds like your mind is feeding on not knowing. What else do you have going on?" Gargi joined the choir that week and started sleeping better.

Before that, Nazia had received message after message, each a little more intense. She felt uneasy, especially when Gargi seemed to know where she had been. She wrote once, clearly: "I'm not interested, and I'd like you to stop messaging me." Then she stopped replying. When the messages kept coming, she saved screenshots, told her roommate, and then went to the hostel warden, who listened and said, "None of this is your fault. I'll talk with both of you today." The warden did, and by the evening the messages had stopped.

Gargi was quiet at the choir practice the next day. She felt ashamed and tender. She did not message Nazia again.

qa.q: What did Gargi join that week?
qa.a: Gargi joined the choir.

qa.q: How did Gargi's looping thoughts and Nazia's unease connect, and what stopped it?
qa.a: Gargi checked Nazia's profile constantly and messaged her, while Nazia felt uneasy, said one clear no, stopped replying, saved screenshots and told her roommate and the warden. Gargi, with Nandini's help, widened her life, and the warden spoke to both that day.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when Gargi seemed to know where she had been?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and unsafe, because the attention was unwanted and too intense.

qa.q: What could Gargi do if the pull to check Nazia's profile comes back?
qa.a: She could remember that it feeds on not knowing, put her time into the choir and friends, and talk to Nandini again.

grounding: An intense crush is seen from the person whose thoughts loop about someone and the person who receives the unwanted attention.

passage:
Saurabh had switched the packaging supplier without telling Reena. The new one was cheaper, and it had felt so obvious that he'd skipped the conversation. For a week he had an uneasy stone in his stomach. He knew that "it saves us money" was not going to fix it. On Thursday he walked into the office early. "I changed the supplier without asking you, and I shouldn't have. I'll switch back until we decide together, and from now on anything over a small limit goes to both of us."

Reena blinked. She was not angry, exactly. Because on the investor call the week before, she had presented the new dashboard as her own work, and Saurabh had built most of it. She realised, sitting there, that she had wronged him too, and that he was hurt. The thought "but you hid something first" rose in her, and she set it aside. "You're right about the supplier. And I owe you something: I took credit for your dashboard on Monday. I'll email the investors today and correct it. If you want to change how we present things, I'll accept that."

Ritu, their advisor, saw them at the whiteboard later, sketching a decision list with both their names on it. She smiled, and left them to it.

qa.q: What did Saurabh change without telling Reena?
qa.a: He switched the packaging supplier.

qa.q: How did Saurabh's coming clean and Reena's admission fit together?
qa.a: Saurabh confessed the supplier change early, offered to switch back and set a shared rule. Reena set aside the thought that he had hidden something first, owned taking credit for the dashboard, and offered to correct it with the investors.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling during the week before he told Reena?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and guilty, like a stone in his stomach.

qa.q: What could Reena do if Saurabh is still hurt about the investor call after her email?
qa.a: She could accept the consequences without demanding forgiveness, and follow through on how they present work.

grounding: Two co-founders' wrongs are seen from the one who hid a decision and confesses early and the one who took credit and owns it without blaming.
